strengths: The paper addresses an important interpretability vulnerability. Shaping feature-visualization trajectories through weight fine-tuning, without architectural additions, is a useful and distinctive attack construction.

Selected demonstrations are convincing. For ResNet-50, target CLIP similarity increases from 0.53 to 0.68 with a one-percentage-point accuracy loss. The CLIP case study produces a recognizable penguin visualization while retaining the assault-rifle feature’s reported AUROC.
Experiments cover several CNN and transformer settings and investigate preservation weight, model size, and target-image choice. The figures and toy example communicate the mechanism clearly.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including hyperparameters, data sources, visualization protocols, and compute requirements; a code link is supplied. Limitations and dual-use implications are explicitly discussed, with no evident unresolved material ethical concern.
weaknesses: The mathematical objective is inconsistent as written. Integrating Eq. (3) gives C − (γ/2)||qᵗ−q||², whereas Eq. (4) has a positive quadratic term; Eq. (10) likewise fits a positive squared-distance function. For the positive γ values used, these functions repel gradient ascent from the target. This may be a transcription error, but the implemented objective must be clarified because both transformer experiments use Eq. (10).

The convergence argument is not adequately connected to practical sampling. Lemma 3.1 assumes initialization inside the slingshot ball and an exact gradient field. Tables 9 and 12 specify both ball radius and coordinatewise initialization standard deviation as 0.01 for ImageNet settings, although the typical Euclidean initialization norm scales as 0.01√d. The norm or sampling convention needs reconciliation. Finite-sample fitting also does not establish the exact gradient condition assumed by the lemma.

Preservation of internal representations and feature function is insufficiently demonstrated. Accuracy and one-versus-rest AUROC can remain stable while other responses change. In the CLIP experiment, w=1 removes the full-representation preservation term, and penguin AUROC increases from 0.50 to 0.62. Held-out activation comparisons and more detailed concept-selectivity measurements are needed to support the central distinction between manipulating an explanation and changing the feature itself.

Evidence for arbitrary replacement across architectures is uneven. At the selected ViT-L/32 setting in Table 16, CLIP similarity decreases from 0.52 to 0.50 and LPIPS worsens from 0.74 to 0.77, which does not quantitatively support successful manipulation. Most settings examine one output feature, with only one constructed internal direction. The 100 or 30 visualization restarts measure visualization variability, rather than reliability across independently trained attacks and diverse feature–target pairs.

The added value of the tunnel construction is not isolated experimentally. Appendix A provides conceptual comparisons, but there is no quantitative comparison with closely related fine-tuning attacks or a simpler target-only objective, and no controlled ablation of tunnel versus endpoint training. Comparisons at matched accuracy and preservation budgets would better establish the methodological contribution.

The defense and auditing conclusions exceed their evaluation. Pre/post top-image Jaccard overlap measures ranking preservation, rather than attack-detection performance. No detection rule, benign controls, or false-positive/false-negative measurements are provided. Furthermore, the proposed sparse-autoencoder and attribution audit is described rather than executed, leaving the claim that discovering the concealed flaw becomes effectively impossible unsupported.
